title: State Management with NgRx & Component Store

questions.prompt: What is the difference between an action and a reducer in NgRx?

options.text: An action mutates state; a reducer describes an event
An action is a plain object describing that something happened; a reducer is a pure function computing new state from state + action

questions.explanation: Actions carry intent with no logic; reducers purely derive the next state, never mutating the existing state.

questions.prompt: Match each NgRx building block to its responsibility.

pairs.right: Performs side effects like HTTP and dispatches results

questions.explanation: These four pieces implement the unidirectional Redux data flow that makes state changes traceable.

questions.prompt: Where should HTTP/API calls happen in an NgRx app?

options.text: Inside effects, which then dispatch success/failure actions

questions.explanation: Isolating side effects in effects keeps reducers pure and preserves the traceable action-to-API narrative.

questions.prompt: When should you choose ComponentStore over the global Store?

options.text: For state shared across many unrelated features
For state local to one component or small feature (filters, pagination, UI flags)
Never — always use the global Store

questions.explanation: ComponentStore keeps local state reactive and immutable without adding global actions/reducers.

questions.prompt: How do you scope a ComponentStore to a single component instance?

options.text: Add it to that component's own providers array

questions.explanation: Providing it in the component's providers ties its lifecycle to that instance; providedIn: 'root' would make it an app-wide singleton.

questions.prompt: Which @ngrx/operators helper safely handles success/error inside an effect so an error doesn't terminate the effect's source stream?
questions.explanation: A plain catchError that rethrows can kill the effect; tapResponse separates next/error handling safely.
